subject: grace-reiter
research_tasks: Research log (2026-10-16, first run, mode create; the baseline was empty and there were no research notes or prior evidence). Leads: the backlog queue note (SNL Season 52 featured player; hometown conflict Madison vs Chippewa Falls; the podcast as main first-person record; Rolling Stone creators list). Opened about 20 web sources and the full podcast feed. Transcribed and read in full 38 long-form recordings (about 30 hours, roughly 350,000 words): 35 YouTube auto-caption transcripts (all 2025-2026 That's Enough episodes available, plus guest appearances on The Downside x2, Couch Surfing, Volley for Serve x2, Literally Life Changing, The Yvette Show, Business Casual Comedy, Wild Wild Web, Page Six, Kyle MacLachlan, I Never Liked You, The Comment Section), Whisper transcriptions of the Hunger Games making-of and two Passion Pod interviews (June 2022, December 2024). Readers extracted timestamped items; every quotation used in claims was rechecked against the transcript text. Evidence was gathered before a type was chosen.

Outcome: status ready, profile_format standard, leading read Type 6 at medium confidence, Type 3 the strongest alternative; Types 1, 9, 2, 7 and 4 tested and set aside (see type_hypothesis). Open-case format considered and rejected: her TikTok breakout dates to 2019-2020 and the first-person record is deep (four years, 30+ hours, plus testimony from her father, sister, roommate, producer and collaborators), so this is a hard typing, not a young record. Risks: contested_typing (Type 6 vs Type 3 is close and the record is comic) and sensitive_allegations (see the sensitivity task); the six-role jury applies.

Accuracy check (2026-10-16). SNL Season 52 began September 26, 2026; she has appeared in each of the first three episodes (C13). SNL was not allowing her to give interviews as of September 17 and no post-casting interview was found (C13). Minimum Wage premieres on Netflix October 26, 2026 (C14). Twilight (but better) was shot in June 2026 and is not yet released (C15). The podcast has had no new episodes since May 11, 2026 (C08). Corrections to common sources: born in the Madison area, not Chippewa Falls (C01); podcast launched March 2025, not late 2024 (C08); full-time American High from 2023 (C07); never lived in LA long-term (C06); no ADHD diagnosis stated (C40); TIME100 Creators claim unverified (C38).

Drafting guidance. Lead with a concrete, sourced moment rather than the SNL announcement, for durability: for example the May 2025 overshare in which the comic famous for gross-out confessions chose as her "real" overshare that she feels "so guilty with the success I have" (C16), or her father's nickname "the shakes" for a girl who now performs live on SNL (C23). Make the argument through the praise-and-success pattern (C16-C19), then the vigilance and checking pattern (C20-C22), then how she steadies herself (C23, C25, C26, C34). Put Type 3 beside the main argument with its real evidence (C05, C30-C32) and say plainly what the discriminator is and where it is weak. Include the boldness and novelty she shows (C36, C37) and the bossy-older-sister material (C27) as complications, not footnotes. Use the SNL, Netflix and Twilight dates as context, not as the hook. Keep "## What is Grace Reiter's personality type?" with an answer of at most 60 words that says Type 6 is the leading read, with Type 3 the closest alternative. Do not claim a wing or subtype; none is defensible. Set enneagram: 6 and published: false.

Sensitivity. (a) Sexuality and romance: across episodes she describes her orientation and romantic history as uncertain and personal, mostly in jokes; do not state or imply an orientation, relationship status or sexual history, and do not use the refused-kiss story beyond, at most, her own short line (C24). (b) Health: no diagnosis (C40); her therapy (C28) may be mentioned only as she framed it publicly, briefly; body-image remarks recur and must not be used as evidence. (c) Substances: a first-weed-experience story and joke references to paranoia or "schizophrenia" are comic and must not be presented as health disclosures. (d) A story about selling non-explicit novelty videos to a fan who then sent an explicit message (The Downside, January 2025) involves a private person; omit. (e) Third-party allegations inside her stories (a high-school classmate described as abusive to a girlfriend; a cousin's criminal charge) concern private people; never repeat them. (f) Family: her mother wants privacy (S32); her grandmother's dementia (S39) and the family dog's death are private; her parents may be named once. (g) Molly's own anxiety and health disclosures in S32 are hers, not Grace's.

Quotation cautions. All transcripts are YouTube auto-captions without speaker names or Whisper transcriptions without speaker labels; check every printed quotation against the audio at the timestamp and remove only clear stutters. Known traps: the "becoming a Christian" overshare is Grace's (verified by context), even though a Stapleview clip of the same conversation is easily misread as the guest's; the ADHD and Adderall lines in S27 are Gianmarco Soresi's; the full-frontal story in S33 is the host's; the "shy older sister", King George III and NFL stories in S47 are Drew Afualo's; in the Passion Pod episodes "control freak" and metrics anxiety are the host's; Whisper renders "Hunger Games" as "Hongka Games" at the start of S31. Censored words appear as "[ __ ]"; quote them with the original bracket or a clearly marked substitution, not a guessed spelling. The January 6 answer in S40 and the dinosaur body-standards premise in S45 are bits. Cite the syndicated NYT copy (S09) that was read, not the unopened original (S49).

Follow-up for the next refresh: (1) transcribe the Eve Hartley interview about Twilight (but better) (S50) and any release-week interviews once Twilight is posted; (2) look for her first post-casting long-form interview, especially how she describes SNL's pressure, feedback and whether she feels she belongs; (3) after October 26, 2026, check Minimum Wage credits and reception; (4) transcribe That's Enough episodes that were not available as YouTube transcripts (Eps 2, 5, 6, 9-13, 19, 21, 27, 28, 31, 33, 36, 39, 44 and the remaining feed-only episodes, IP-blocked on 2026-10-16), the Gaydar episode, the Spooners short and the 2021 Drew Barrymore Show segment; (5) seek testimony from American High (Will Phelps, the Micho brothers, Julia DiCesare) or SNL colleagues; (6) confirm the Rolling Stone rank and whether a TIME100 Creators listing exists.

claims.claim: Grace Marie Reiter was born on May 18, 2001, in the Madison area of Wisconsin and grew up in Chippewa Falls, where her family moved in 2007; she started first grade at Southview Elementary and graduated from Chippewa Falls High School in 2019.
claims.inference: Her father (via the Leader-Telegram) says the family lived in Madison, where she was born, and moved back in 2007. Wikipedia gives the full date and cites a Capital Times St. Mary's Hospital birth notice and Chippewa Herald birthday notices (not opened). In 2022 she said she was "born in Verona, just a little south of Madison" and moved back "like in first grade". Safe wording: born in the Madison area (or "near Madison"), raised in Chippewa Falls.
claims.alternative: Milwaukee Magazine says "born and raised in Chippewa Falls" and trade outlets say "originally from Chippewa Falls"; those are wrong or loose on birthplace. Verona versus a Madison hospital is unresolved; do not print a city of birth more precise than the Madison area. The full date rests on Wikipedia's cited notices plus Russh; it is consistent with her age (25 in September 2026).

claims.claim: Her parents are Tim and Valerie Reiter, both 1991 graduates of Chippewa Falls High School; her younger sister Molly appears in some of her videos and in the Hunger Games parody, and her father says he never misses her videos.
claims.inference: Family facts from the hometown paper; Molly is an on-record participant (S32).
claims.alternative: Parents are private people. Name them only where necessary; her mother has said (via Molly) that she dislikes appearing in podcast stories.

claims.claim: Her father describes a lifelong appetite for performance and attention and calls SNL a goal she held "forever": "She's always been a ham for the camera, and loved attention. She's always been funny," and "It's been her goal forever." He recalls her telling him, "Dad, I'm getting a lot of fans on this. I think I might be TikTok famous." Family members told local TV that once "she knew that she could make somebody laugh, it was over."
claims.inference: Independent of her own self-presentation and consistent with her account of making videos since middle school. It supports a long-held drive to perform; it does not by itself say what motive drives it.
claims.alternative: A proud parent speaking on the day of a career milestone; attention-loving in childhood is common and is not type-specific (Types 2, 3, 6 and 7 can all present this way).

claims.claim: Her school performing history is contested: the Leader-Telegram says she "never got involved in plays or musicals in school," but she says she played Elizabeth Proctor in a high-school production of The Crucible, and she tells of an eighth-grade choir solo that she presents as the origin of her stage fright.
claims.inference: Her own specific account (role, a real coughing fit on stage) outweighs a general line in a news story; the newspaper may mean she was not a regular in the drama program.
claims.alternative: Do not print "she never did theater" as fact. Either attribute both accounts or omit.

claims.claim: In 2022, at 20, she described her ambition in terms of online identity: "I grew up in the YouTube era. YouTubers were my celebrities. I think my dream had always been to be an Internet persona." She also said the persona carries pressure: "you have to be this persona and you don't want to overthink it ... Because that's what made people like you in the first place."
claims.inference: Early evidence that being seen and liked online was the goal, and that she felt the liked self had to be maintained. The second quote expresses fear of losing what made people like her.
claims.alternative: Read as Type 3 (identity fused with an image that wins approval), this is the strongest early evidence for the alternative. Read as Type 6, it is worry about losing approval she cannot trust. A 20-year-old describing the creator economy accurately also explains it.

claims.claim: She was an original cast member of Stapleview, a live TikTok sketch show created by former Broadway Video producer Sam Grey that premiered March 3, 2022 and was filmed in Los Angeles; she then lived in a short-term sublet in LA, not a permanent move.
claims.inference: Contemporaneous reporting. In 2022 and 2024 she describes the LA stint as about three months and says she never moved there.
claims.alternative: The Leader-Telegram says she "moved to Burbank, Calif." after graduating; that most likely describes the Stapleview stint. Avoid saying she lived in LA long-term.

claims.claim: American High, a Syracuse-area film company, recruited her as a guest around February 2023 and hired her full-time around July 2023 as one of five core cast members of American High Shorts and College Life, relocating her to Syracuse; by fall 2024 she was no longer part of the shorts, and she moved to New York City in December 2024. She did not attend Syracuse University.
claims.inference: Her own consistent dating ("July of 2023 to October 2024", S33; guest about February 2023 and full-time about July 2023, S19) plus contemporaneous Daily Orange and Panther reporting. NYC move from S20 (arrived about December 9, 2024) and S30.
claims.alternative: Wikipedia and CNY Central say she joined in late 2022 (Phelps began trialing comedians in October 2022). She still appears in Minimum Wage, an American High production. Use "2023" or "from 2023" for the full-time role.

claims.claim: Her podcast "That's Enough with Grace Reiter" (Stapleview) ran weekly from March 31, 2025 (trailer March 28) to April 13, 2026, then ended with best-of compilations through May 11, 2026; its premise was "oversharing."
claims.inference: RSS feed dates. Wikipedia's "late 2024" launch date is wrong.
claims.alternative: The show may resume; no announcement was found. Episodes were often published months after recording, so use recording context, not publish date, for chronology.
claims.review_trigger: If new That's Enough episodes appear after May 11, 2026, update the run dates.

claims.claim: She made "The Hunger Games (but better)," a roughly 42- to 45-minute parody she directed and starred in as Katniss, with friends over three days around her 24th birthday in May 2025, and posted it on YouTube on November 19, 2025; it had about 13 to 14 million views by September 2026. In the making-of video she says she did it because "I want to be Katniss for my birthday, I want to be the lead in a movie for my birthday."
claims.inference: Release date and views from her channel and press; motive line is her own narration (S31, check audio because Whisper misheard the title).
claims.alternative: View counts are time-sensitive; write "more than 13 million views by September 2026". She also frames the project as a gift to her friends and says the idea came from improvising with friends (C34), so "she wanted to be the lead" should not stand alone.

claims.claim: She plans her projects exhaustively and enjoys controlling the details: for the parody she watched the film pausing at every cut to build a shot list and spreadsheet ("I'm a nerd... I like spreadsheets"), cast every role herself ("I casted everybody perfectly"), timed the release to the franchise calendar, and describes "micromanaging everything" on set as fun.
claims.inference: Repeated across November 2025 to September 2026 and confirmed by an interviewer who mentions her "binders", "spreadsheets" and "presentations" (S34). Preparation and control are a reliable feature of her work.
claims.alternative: Planning fits several types: Type 6 (preparation as safety; she says practicing made her "not even nervous at all" before the 2024 SNL showcase, S19), Type 3 (efficient execution toward a goal) and Type 1 (getting it right). It does not discriminate on its own.

claims.claim: On HBO's The Chair Company (premiered October 2025), created by and starring Tim Robinson, she played Tara, the "controlling, abrasive" fiancee of Robinson's character's daughter, in six episodes. She says she was too intimidated to talk to Robinson much and afterward felt "I tricked them all."
claims.inference: Role facts from the NYT and Wikipedia; her account of freezing and feeling like an impostor is self-report from two separate interviews.
claims.alternative: The character's abrasiveness is a role, not evidence about her. Impostor feelings are common in first big jobs.

claims.claim: She went through the SNL audition process twice: a 2024 showcase (self-tape, then a five-minute character set) that did not lead to a hire, and the summer 2026 showcases and screen tests, after which NBC named her a featured player for Season 52 on September 16, 2026, alongside Saidah Belo-Osagie. At 25 she is the first cast member born in the 21st century.
claims.inference: Her own 2024 account of the first showcase plus Deadline and NYT reporting of the 2026 hire. In 2024 she called SNL "the dream" but said "I don't know if I could handle that work" and preferred "one and done" projects.
claims.alternative: Her 2024 showcase outcome is inferred from the record (she never says she advanced, and she was not hired); do not claim she was "rejected" in stronger terms than that. Her father says SNL invited her to the 2026 showcase.
claims.review_trigger: Revisit at the end of Season 52 (about May 2027): contract renewal, promotion to repertory, or departure.

claims.claim: In the Season 52 premiere (September 26, 2026) a recap noted "Reiter landing an unexpectedly high number of appearances as a rookie"; in October she appeared in "Get Ready with Me" (Dakota Johnson episode) and played an elderly mother in hospice opposite Shane Gillis in "Saying Goodbye." As of September 17, 2026, SNL was not allowing her to give media interviews, and no post-casting interview was found by October 16, 2026.
claims.inference: Three episodes in. Performance roles are not personality evidence; the interview restriction explains the gap in post-casting first-person material.
claims.alternative: Early-season screen time fluctuates; do not build the argument on it.
claims.review_trigger: Check for her first post-casting long-form interview (likely during the season or at the end of it) and for any critical assessment of her SNL work.

claims.claim: Netflix ordered 28 episodes (about 12.5 minutes each) of American High's "Minimum Wage," adapted from the 2024 web series in which she plays Grace; the series premieres October 26, 2026, and she is credited by Deadline and the NYT as a writer and director on it. She says the writers' room began in January 2026 and the shoot wrapped June 5, 2026.
claims.inference: Order and premiere from trade and NYT reporting; schedule from her own account.
claims.alternative: Variety gives the 28-episode order; check how many episodes are released on October 26. Her exact writing/directing credits should be checked against Netflix's credits after release.
claims.review_trigger: After the October 26, 2026 premiere: confirm credits, episode count released, and reception.

claims.claim: "Twilight (but better)," her follow-up parody, was shot the week after Minimum Wage wrapped in June 2026 and was unreleased on her channel as of October 16, 2026; she says she cried after the shoot and apologized to her volunteer cast: "I'm so sorry I made you guys do that. It was so long. It was so hard."
claims.inference: Her own account of shooting dates and her reaction; release status checked on her channel.
claims.alternative: Release timing may simply be post-production. The apology fits guilt and responsibility toward a group (Types 6, 1 or 2) but is also ordinary decency toward unpaid friends.
claims.review_trigger: When Twilight (but better) is released, update the status and check her release-week interviews (including the unopened Eve Hartley interview, S50).

claims.claim: Her May 2025 "overshare" on her own podcast was guilt about success: "I feel so guilty with the success I have. I'm thinking about becoming a Christian." She explained that when people praise her, "I'm like, 'I can't handle this.' And I'm like, 'But if I believed in God, I could give all of it to God,'" and that "the ego can get so so large. And that's what I'm terrified of."
claims.inference: She sets aside her usual gross-out overshares to offer this as the real one, and seven months later her roommate refers back to it unprompted ("why you wanted to find God", S42), so it reflects something persistent, not a one-off bit. It shows praise experienced as a weight she wants an outside authority to carry.
claims.alternative: Delivered with laughter and a riff on celebrity conversions; partly comic. Midwestern modesty and a young person's surprise at fast success are plausible circumstantial explanations. A Type 3 concerned with not appearing vain could say the first sentence, but the wish for an external authority to "give all of it" to fits Type 6 better. She later said she simply stopped thinking about the religion idea (S42).

claims.claim: People close to her describe active discomfort with praise: her roommate Max Zavidow says "you hate compliments more than anyone I know," and when he starts to praise her on her podcast she cuts him off ("we can't do this on my podcast") and calls herself in "attack mode"; Drew Afualo tells her "You're wincing when you say it"; on Gianmarco Soresi's podcast she answers a compliment with "Thank you for the compliment. I'm sorry."
claims.inference: Independent observers in three settings (December 2025 to September 2026) plus observed behavior. This is the core of the discriminator against Type 3: approval is deflected rather than taken in.
claims.alternative: Comic self-deprecation is a professional technique she names ("comedy 101... just shit on yourself", S27), and deflecting compliments is a Midwestern social norm. Max adds she is getting better at it ("I feel like I'm good at it now"). She also says "I want the attention but I also don't want to ask for it" (S41), so the aversion is to direct praise, not to attention itself.

claims.claim: She frames her talent as something she should not own or enjoy: told by Busy Philipps that she is "big" in the Philipps house, she said "I don't think you're allowed to perceive yourself like that... Like I'm for you guys," and cited Madonna on being "the manager of your talent" so as not to tie "selfworth to... the views and the likes." Asked what she is working on, she said, "I never tell people any of the stuff I do because I don't want them to come."
claims.inference: Consistent with C16 and C17 (November and December 2025). Shows a deliberate strategy for holding success at a distance; the Business Casual line (December 2025, three hosts, attribution medium) shows reluctance to draw attention to her own work.
claims.alternative: A healthy, borrowed philosophy of craft could explain it without any type-specific anxiety; it is also what a Type 3 trying not to be ruled by metrics might adopt.

claims.claim: She expects success to be followed by a fall and fears what it might make her: in January 2025 she called being a narcissist her "biggest fear," and in February 2026, after the parody's success, she said "something's going to happen and it is my own hand that brings down myself."
claims.inference: Anticipating danger at the moment of success is a Type 6 signature; a Type 3 more typically fears failure and being seen failing, not success itself.
claims.alternative: Both lines are half-jokes (the narcissism line follows a TikTok-trivia joke; the "own hand" line is about an embarrassing overshare in that episode), and the narcissism attribution is medium. Treat as supporting, not decisive.

claims.claim: She repeatedly anticipates other people's judgment and checks for it: on her own oversharing show she asks "Why did I make this whole podcast over sharing when everything I over share I'm like, 'Is that okay?'"; after an embarrassing night she asked friends "Do you guys think of me differently now?"; she says "I just like hope my friends are actually my friends," "I'm always like someone they're going to be mean to me and they never are," and declines opinion shows because "I don't want to be judged for my opinion."
claims.inference: Five contexts from December 2025 to August 2026, including both guest and host settings. The pattern is vigilance about hidden disapproval and disloyalty, followed by reality-checking, which fits Type 6 more closely than Type 3 (whose fear centers on failing publicly rather than on whether people are secretly against them).
claims.alternative: Fear of judgment is near-universal among young performers with large comment sections; she cried over a "women aren't funny" comment early on (S18, S28). Several lines come with self-mockery.

claims.claim: She calls herself a people pleaser who is "so afraid of like offending people" that she holds back ("I think I would go further"), and she keeps sharp private judgments to herself for the same reason; her roommate calls her "one of the all-time great haters."
claims.inference: The gap between private judgment and public restraint is explained by fear of consequences, which fits Type 6 (and also Types 1, 2 and 9). The roommate's testimony shows the restraint is not the absence of strong opinions.
claims.alternative: Type 2 people-pleasing aims at being liked and needed; nothing in the record shows her seeking to be needed (she says "please text me cuz like I won't text you", C29). Type 9 conflict-avoidance would not usually coexist with this much private sharpness.

claims.claim: She describes being afraid of confrontation: asked whether she blows up, she said "I think it's more so I'm just afraid of confrontation too and like like making someone upset," and told of a complaint to an American High roommate that "spilled out of me because I was so nervous to tell him" in front of everyone at breakfast.
claims.inference: A specific behavioral story with its cost (an awkward public moment) and her own causal reading ("you build it up in your head of like, oh my god, he's going to think I'm like attacking him").
claims.alternative: Single source for the story; conflict-avoidance is shared by Types 2, 6 and 9. It sits beside self-described bluntness ("I'm very like blunt or like curt", S36), which is the counterphobic side of the same pattern or simply Midwestern directness.

claims.claim: She traces lifelong stage fright to an eighth-grade choir solo, after which her father nicknamed her "the shakes": "I don't think he understood how personally or how much that was going to affect me." She has told the story in January 2025, July 2025 and April 2026, and says characters and preparation make performing feel safe.
claims.inference: A durable, repeated self-account of fear of being watched, managed through structure (characters, practice). In 2024 she prepared nightly at open mics for the SNL showcase and "was like, not even nervous at all" (S19).
claims.alternative: Stage fright is common and partly physiological; hosts note she "immediately get[s] shy" (S45). It is evidence of anxiety, not of a specific type, except in how she manages it (preparation and roles).

claims.claim: She describes herself as cautious: "I'm not a risk taker... I'm protecting myself" (on four-wheelers, March 2025), and in March 2026 said she refused a kiss "cuz I was scared," adding "I have to stop living in fear."
claims.inference: Self-described protective caution across physical and personal situations, a year apart.
claims.alternative: Counterevidence: her comedy takes social risks (gross-out videos, an oversharing podcast, a 45-minute parody), and she moved cities for work. The mix of caution and bold content fits a Type 6 phobic/counterphobic oscillation but also fits a performer whose risks are taken only inside a role. The kiss story is romantic and sensitive; use at most in her words, briefly.

claims.claim: She describes a long habit of under-effort she attributes to fear: "I don't know if it's necessarily a fear of failure... maybe like a fear of actually trying... I feel like my whole life I've kind of half halfass everything," adding that "the fear is actually being successful." In 2022 she called herself "a procrastinator and a lazy person at heart" who was "going to like coast," and in 2024 said she works best when "somebody else is like, hey, you have to do this."
claims.inference: Four years of consistent self-description. Needing an external obligation to act, and fearing the stakes of full effort, fit Type 6 (and Type 9); they fit Type 3 and Type 1 poorly.
claims.alternative: Her output contradicts the label: a year of 9-to-6 sketch production, a podcast every week for a year, a self-produced feature-length parody, nightly open mics before the showcase. The laziness may be a self-image, not a behavior. In 2024 she called it "executive dysfunction"; she has stated no diagnosis (C40).

claims.claim: She seeks outside guidance and structure: she wrote in her journal "I want a teacher. I want a mentor. I want a father" (adding that she wrote the last part mostly because it sounded "poetic"), wants a therapist she can look up to, and says of her parents, "If anything I wish they punished me more."
claims.inference: A wish for a trustworthy authority to lean on is a central Type 6 theme and ties to C16 (giving success "to God").
claims.alternative: She explicitly frames "I want a father" as poetic license, not a complaint about her own father, whom she describes warmly. Young artists commonly want mentors. The punishment line was partly said to reassure Busy Philipps, who had called herself a bad mom.

claims.claim: She takes charge on her own projects and describes herself as a bossy older sister who enforces seriousness, then quickly checks on the people she corrected: "I'm the one friend that's like no but like we have to take this serious you guys"; "sometimes I'm like such a [b---h] where... I would shut that down immediately... And that's not fair," followed by "have I given you a complex about this?" Her producer is "proud of you for taking the lead."
claims.inference: Shows real assertiveness when responsible for a group, coupled with fast repair and worry about hurting people. The repair-and-reassure step fits Type 6 (and Type 2) better than Type 8 or Type 1 certainty.
claims.alternative: Type 1 would explain the enforcement of standards ("we have to take this serious", "we have to follow the rules. We have to be good", S33) and her self-labeling; Type 3 would explain driving the product. Directing a low-budget shoot with friends also simply requires someone to be in charge.

claims.claim: She is harshly self-critical: she brought her therapist "a list of like all like the mistakes I made today" and concluded "I guess I'm just like the worst person in the world" (February 2026); in 2022 she said the LA trip taught her "maybe I'm not an awful horrible person"; she calls herself "a total [b---h] all the time," and her sister agrees she "was just a general [b---h] for most of my life" ("it was really hard to go on vacations with you").
claims.inference: A persistent, four-year thread of self-condemnation and review of her own conduct toward others. Gianmarco Soresi: "you're a completely non-functional human being. Yet you produce, you don't miss things."
claims.alternative: This is the strongest evidence for Type 1 (an inner critic reviewing mistakes). Against Type 1: her self-review asks whether she hurt or offended people rather than whether she did things correctly, she seeks others' reassurance rather than relying on an inner standard (C20), and she describes half-effort and mess tolerance a Type 1 would not accept (C25). Much of the sibling material is affectionate teasing; therapy content is sensitive and should be summarized lightly.

claims.claim: She keeps people at a distance despite being sociable on camera: "maybe like I fear intimacy," her friendships come in a "burst of time" and fade, and she asked American High friends to "please text me cuz like I won't text you... I don't want to feel like needy."
claims.inference: Sincere answers under questioning. Fear of seeming needy argues against a Type 2 reading. Ambivalence about closeness is compatible with Type 6 (trust takes time) and with a touring performer's life.
claims.alternative: Circumstance: frequent moves (Chippewa Falls, LA sublet, Eau Claire, Syracuse, New York) make "burst" friendships structural, as she says herself. Romantic history is private and should not be used as evidence.

claims.claim: Her ambition has a moving target: "the goalpost is always moving cuz once I hit 1 million, I was like, 'Yeah, but like all the really Tik Tok famous people have 3 million,'" "it'll never... be enough," "I'm always saying I could do more, be bigger, go harder"; she went to the Mall of America early in her fame because "I feel like I have to get recognized by someone," and said of a parody, "If I don't get a million, I'm actually going to be really really embarrassed."
claims.inference: Repeated from April 2025 to August 2026. This is the core of the Type 3 alternative: metrics and recognition as yardsticks of worth, with escalating goals.
claims.alternative: For Type 6 the same ladder reads as an inability to feel arrived or safe ("It never feels real", "imposter syndrome", S22). She also says she avoids looking at numbers and wants to stop tying worth to "views and likes" (C18). In 2022 she withheld her analytics from her manager because her TikTok was underperforming (S18), which can be read as image protection (Type 3) or fear of judgment (Type 6).

claims.claim: She works constantly and struggles to enjoy results: "I don't take time to really process or enjoy anything. I'm just like work mode all the time" (August 2026) and "I don't like let myself enjoy anything" (September 2026); in 2024 she said she gets most stressed "when I'm not doing stuff."
claims.inference: A Type 3 pattern (doing over feeling) and also consistent with Type 6 restlessness and anxiety when idle.
claims.alternative: Her 2024 self-description was "floating... thing to thing" and "I'm having fun"; the 2026 lines come in her busiest year (Netflix series, Twilight, SNL audition), so circumstance explains part of it.

claims.claim: Some of her statements tie her sense of self to performing: "I feel like I don't exist unless I mean funny," which she immediately reframed as "when I'm... being funny and hanging out with friends... I'm existing and I'm present"; asked how she labels herself, she said "people tell me things about me and I'm just like I don't know. Like I guess I'm truly just a shell."
claims.inference: The plainest evidence that could support Type 3 (identity located in the performed self). In context the first is about presence with friends and the second is a deadpan aside about how others label her sexuality.
claims.alternative: She rejects a compulsion to get laughs ("This is something I enjoy", S25) and says she can be quiet and have a good time. Do not use the "shell" line as a thesis; it is a joke answer on a sensitive topic.

claims.claim: Her oversharing is selective: she says "the real overshare stuff would be like sad and like not funny," "nobody knows me and nobody knows actually really what I'm feeling," and "I don't want to tell these people all this stuff. That's why I have default to [gross-out humor]"; her producer says she has only ever asked for one cut, made to protect another person.
claims.inference: The gross-out persona works as a shield for private feeling; she guards others' privacy more than her own dignity.
claims.alternative: Any type can keep private material private; this argues against reading her podcast as unfiltered self-revelation, not for a particular type. A Type 4 reading (feeling unknown) was tested and set aside: she withholds rather than cultivates the sadness and does not make difference or longing her subject.

claims.claim: She consistently shares credit and describes her dream as making things with friends: "it wasn't really my idea it was all of our idea cuz we were improvising"; "I just want to make a movie with my friends"; in 2024 she prayed in gratitude and wished for "little indie films with my friends."
claims.inference: Belonging to a trusted group is central to her account of what she wants (American High was "everything", S33), consistent with Type 6 loyalty and also with Type 2 and Type 9 group orientation.
claims.alternative: She also takes pride in specific credit ("I casted everybody perfectly", S32) and in being the lead (C09). Sharing credit is also good collaborative practice.

claims.claim: Colleagues describe her as earnest and serious under the chaos: her producer says "You do take things very seriously... you're taking people at your word... You're so earnestly here"; Julia DiCesare says "rigid is the last word people would use to describe you" as a performer even though Grace sees herself as rigid; Drew Afualo calls her "rigid and shy."
claims.inference: Independent testimony from close collaborators across 2025-2026 about trustingness and seriousness. Taking people at their word is notable for a Type 6 reading because it shows trust once given, not universal suspicion.
claims.alternative: Supports Types 1 and 6 about equally; "earnest" is also how her comedy is marketed (Rolling Stone, S12).

claims.claim: She also seeks novelty and resists repetition: "I just need like novelty"; she keeps "a couple projects going on at a time" so there is "something else to immediately move on to"; she prefers "one and done" projects and says "let's do the next thing."
claims.inference: A real feature of her working style that the Type 6 reading does not explain well; Type 7 and Type 3 explain it better. It may also be a way of managing anxiety about any single project's reception (she says moving on keeps her from getting "too caught up in the numbers", S22).
claims.alternative: Type 7 was tested and set aside because she reports not letting herself enjoy things (C31), guilt and dread rather than optimism, and fear rather than escape as the driver.

claims.claim: She has defied audience expectations at least once at a cost: after her first viral video (a Harry Styles fan-fiction parody in 2019), she declined to keep making them ("Because the people wanted me to do it. And I said, 'Fuck the people'"), then watched her follower growth plateau and half-regretted it.
claims.inference: A costly choice against audience demand. Counterweight to a pure approval reading (Type 3) and to a purely fearful one.
claims.alternative: Told comically; the regret is also comic ("I should have just kept making Harry Styles fanfiction"). Boredom (C36) may explain it as well as principle.

claims.claim: Rolling Stone placed her on its "25 Most Influential Creators of 2026" (published August 27, 2026), quoting her: "A lot of times I'm making things to be like, 'We all think this, right?'"
claims.inference: List inclusion and a short quote.
claims.alternative: The rank was not visible in the fetched text; the queue note says No. 20. Milwaukee Magazine's claim that she made TIME100 Creators 2026 is unverified; do not use it.

claims.claim: She appeared Off-Broadway in "Ginger Twinsies," a Parent Trap parody at the Orpheum Theatre that ran from July to October 2025, playing Chessy and other roles; she said performing nightly was "awesome" but the repetition wore on her.
claims.inference: Credit from Wikipedia and NYT; reaction from her own account.
claims.alternative: Some coverage dates it as "last year" from 2026; use July-October 2025.

claims.claim: She has not disclosed a diagnosis: asked in September 2025 whether she had been diagnosed with anything, she said "No"; in 2024 she said "I struggle with executive dysfunction." The ADHD and Adderall remarks in her podcast episodes belong to guests (Gianmarco Soresi; the guests of the episode titled "ADHD Podcast").
claims.inference: Prevents a likely misattribution.
claims.alternative: Do not describe her as having ADHD or any condition. If mentioned at all, use her own phrase and date.

type_hypothesis.against: (1) The Type 3 case is substantial: since 2022 she has described her goal as being an "Internet persona" and worried about keeping the persona people liked (C05); she measures herself by followers and views on a ladder that is "never... enough", went to the Mall of America to be recognized, and would be "really really embarrassed" under a million views (C30); she is "work mode all the time" and does not let herself enjoy results (C31); she made the parody partly to "be the lead in a movie" (C09); and she has said "I don't exist unless I mean funny" and "I guess I'm truly just a shell" (C32). (2) The Type 1 case: a daily list of her mistakes for her therapist and "I'm just like the worst person in the world" (C28), "we have to follow the rules. We have to be good" and enforcing seriousness on set (C27), self-described rigidity and taking everything seriously (C35), and moral lines such as refusing to punch down. (3) Circumstance and incentives: self-deprecation is her stated comic method ("comedy 101... just shit on yourself"), Midwestern modesty explains deflecting compliments, and a 23-to-25-year-old whose career jumped from TikTok to HBO, Netflix and SNL in a year has ordinary reasons for impostor feelings and dread (C11, C12). Much of the record is a comedy podcast whose premise is oversharing, so sincerity must be judged line by line, and several key lines (C19, C24) are half-jokes. (4) The evidence for caution and fear sits beside real boldness: gross-out videos, refusing to keep making the content that first went viral (C37), moving cities for work, self-described bluntness, and directing friends firmly (C27). (5) Novelty-seeking and many simultaneous projects (C36) and her self-described "coasting" and procrastination (C25) are not central Type 6 features.
type_hypothesis.alternative_case: Type 3 is the strongest rival because her ambition is explicit, long-running and metric-driven (C05, C30): an early dream of being an online persona, escalating follower goals, recognition-seeking, embarrassment at modest view counts, "work mode all the time" (C31), strategic release planning (C10), and statements that locate her existence in performing (C32). On this reading the praise-deflection (C16-C18) is image management: a self-preserving Three who does not want to look vain, and the guilt is about appearing egotistical. What strains the Type 3 reading: she moves away from approval when it arrives, independently observed by a roommate and a host (C17); she wants an outside authority to carry her success (C16, C26); she predicts her own downfall at the moment of success (C19); she fears trying fully rather than fearing failure (C25) and works best when someone else imposes the obligation; and her characteristic worry is whether people are secretly against her or will be mean to her (C20), not whether she is succeeding. A Three's self-protection usually takes the form of more efficient striving and polished image, not refusing compliments, apologizing for them, and asking "Is that okay?" on her own show. Type 1 was tested: the inner-critic material (C28) is real, but her self-review is about whether she hurt or offended people, she relies on others' reassurance rather than an inner standard, and she describes half-effort and mess tolerance that a One would not accept (C25). Type 9 was tested: coasting, going along with managers' decisions, retreat into video games and comfort TV, and conflict avoidance fit (C22, C25), but she is too vigilant, self-critical and anxious when idle (C31) for Nine. Type 2 was tested: she calls herself a people pleaser (C21) and shares credit (C34), but she avoids seeming needy, does not text first, and shows no pattern of making herself needed (C29). Type 7 (novelty, many projects, C36) and Type 4 (feeling unknown, C33) were tested and set aside: she reports guilt, dread and not letting herself enjoy things rather than optimism, and she withholds rather than cultivates her sadness.
type_hypothesis.discriminator: What she does when approval actually arrives. A Type 3 moves toward admiration, takes it in as confirmation, and converts it into the next goal; a Type 6 treats it as unsettling and potentially dangerous, looks for something trustworthy outside herself to hold it, and braces for the ground to give way. Across May 2025 to September 2026, in host, guest and private-household settings, she does the second: "I can't handle this... if I believed in God, I could give all of it to God" (C16), "I'm for you guys" and talent she is only "the manager of" (C18), compliments answered with "I'm sorry" and a "wince" (C17), and "something's going to happen and it is my own hand that brings down myself" after her biggest hit (C19). Two people with daily access (her roommate) or extended conversation (Drew Afualo) independently describe the aversion. A second, supporting discriminator is where she gets steadiness under pressure: from preparation, obligations set by others, trusted collaborators and a wished-for mentor or authority (C23, C25, C26, C34), and from checking whether people are still with her ("Is that okay?", "Do you guys think of me differently now?", C20), rather than from the audience's applause. Limits: the escalating-goals evidence (C30) does not discriminate, both types fit it; she does use the audience as a gauge of whether material works ("I'm always trying to like make people break cuz I'm like I want I need to know", S46, about a live show), which is ordinary for a comic but is the Type 3 side of the second discriminator; much of the record is comic; and the discriminator rests on a performer's statements in a 17-month window during sudden fame. Hence medium confidence and the full jury.
type_hypothesis.unexplained: Her novelty-seeking and preference for "one and done" projects (C36). The early and persistent dream of being an online persona, and her saying she does not exist unless funny (C05, C32), which Type 3 explains more naturally. Her repeated self-description as lazy and coasting against a record of heavy output (C25). The firmness with which she directs and corrects friends, and her harsh self-labels, beside her fear of confrontation and of offending (C22, C27). Her taking people at their word (C35) beside her worry that friends are secretly mocking her (C20). Her bold, sometimes transgressive comic content beside her self-description as "not a risk taker" (C24, C37). In 2024 she said she did not know if she could handle SNL's workload and preferred one-off projects, then pursued SNL again in 2026 (C12).
